speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT ON LIFE OF POPE JOHN PAUL II
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure that when I make these comments I am expressing the feelings not only of the members of the House but of people throughout Canada in expressing shock and horror at the assassination attempt on the life of His Holiness, Pope John Paul II. Obviously at this stage it is difficult to know the details of this tragic occurrence. It is our hope that we will find as the day develops that the seriousness we now perceive will have been reduced. I should like to tell you, Madam Speaker, and members of the House, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been informed of this assassination attempt and has conveyed a message to the Vatican foreign secretary, Cardinal Casaroli.
It is a chilling irony that a man who has given so much of himself to preaching peace and love throughout the world should himself become the target of such violence. All Canadians, I am sure, will be waiting with hope and joining with us in prayer for the life of Pope John Paul II.

subtopic: ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT ON LIFE OF POPE JOHN PAUL II
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT ON LIFE OF POPE JOHN PAUL II
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to associate myself, my leader, my party, and all of my colleagues in the House with the statement that has been made by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on behalf of the people of the country.
We reacted when we heard of this assassination attempt, and are still reacting, with a sense of shock and sorrow that a man of his stature in the world should be struck down the way in which he was.
Pope John Paul II has inspired people of every religion, race and culture as he has reached out to the whole world in the search that has been his for peace and justice. He has amazed all of us with his vigour, his great warmth for people and how he has been able to touch them. People all over the world, believers and non-believers, have been moved by his messages of hope in which one theme has predominated, that the human right to a life of justice and security implanted in every human being must be achieved and safeguarded by policies and programs of peace.
We pray that this leader will be spared to a world so much in need of his message of faith, hope and love. I associate myself, my party and all of my colleagues, with these remarks. I hope there will be found a way to convey to the Vatican the messages that will come from this House of Commons today. I join with the Deputy Prime Minister in the fervent hope that, as the day unfolds, the prognosis for a full and complete recovery of this great leader of the world will be good.

subtopic: ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT ON LIFE OF POPE JOHN PAUL II
speechtext: Hear, hear!

As has already been indicated, it is tragic that one who has obviously dedicated his life to the furtherance of peace and justice should have been struck down in the worldwide spread of terrorism and violence. I know I speak for all Canadians when I say we wish him a complete and speedy recovery.

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the most basic of all human rights is the right to life, whereas assassinations and terrorism are the most brutal, cowardly and despicable forms of crime and are a radical offence against humanity, whereas the trend to such opprobrious violence has escalated, with assassinations and attempted assassinations, including those aimed at the President of the United States and His Holiness, Pope John Paul II, and whereas the House of Commons unanimously passed a resolution on October 15, 1980, condemning all acts of terrorism anywhere in the world, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne):

Madam Speaker, my question is a supplementary, to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I think today we have seen a very vivid illustration of the irresponsible approach of the government to the economy in the visit of the members of the oil and gas service industry to Ottawa. These companies, which are all Canadian-owned, estimate that 40 per cent of their number will not be in business in six months' time and that about 75 per cent will not be in business in one year's time, if things are not changed in the energy industry. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Since the minister has indicated he has no plans to help agricultural producers cope with high interest rates at the present time, I would like to ask him whether he considers that Ottawa has some responsibility to help the hundreds of farmers who will be forced out of agriculture at the end, or before the end of this year, because of the high interest rates brought on by the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member knows full well that most of the farmers who are in financial difficulty are those who borrowed money from private banking interests. I believe, and I hope the hon. member believes, that the private banking interests also have a responsibility to these people. They are making good profits and can afford to give some of these people moratoriums on their programs. They can afford to give them longer-term mortgages with a moratorium, and amortizing the program later. We suggested that to The Canadian Bankers'
Association. I suggested that to the provincial ministers yesterday.
We are looking at different programs. We will try to adjust the Farm Credit Corporation to help some of these people. It will be impossible to help them all. Those farmers who are in difficulty are outside some kind of orderly marketing system that has a supply management system or a contract system for them, they are the ones in the most difficulty. speechtext: Madam Speaker, that is a callous, silly, stupid answer to a very serious question, from a Minister of Agriculture who should know better. speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Minister of Finance for permitting interest rates to rise to unprecedented high levels and calls on the minister to meet his economic responsibilities or resign.
He said: Madam Speaker, this motion comes forward at a time when the Canadian economy and the people of Canada, the farmers, the fishermen and the businessmen-indeed, all aspects of Canadian life-are threatened by a most serious and unprecedented economic situation, illustrated in particular by unprecedented high interest rates.
It is also a time such as we have never seen before, with a government in Canada which is so unwilling to assume its economic and financial responsibility. This government was elected some 14 months ago on the basis that it could do better than the government which was in power then for a few months, the PC Clark government. It was elected on the basis that it could do better and on the argument that it could keep interest rates down, stimulate the economy and overcome inflation. It was elected on the argument that there was a painless way this could be done.
We have had 14 months of inactivity, 14 months of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) hiding behind the skirts of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the Constitution. We now see the emperor without his clothes. The emperor has been walking down the street without his clothes, hiding behind his constitutional cloak. Yesterday he came out from behind his constitutional cloak and the people of Canada discovered there was nothing there. He was not wearing a shred, but he was still completely unashamed.
The minister said in a speech last week that inflation has been running at the rate of 13.9 per cent. The present inflation rate is 13.9 per cent. In his budget of October 28 he predicted
10.2	per cent; just five months ago the minister predicted a
10.2	per cent inflation rate for 1981. This points out another serious aspect of this situation: the forecasts of the Department of Finance can no longer be trusted. They can no longer be accepted as anywhere near accurate.
In his budget the minister predicted that this year the Canadian dollar would average 87 cents compared to the U.S.
Interest Rates
dollar. Today we see it struggling to keep above 83 cents in terms of the U.S. dollar.
We are now seeing a serious unemployment situation, with the adjusted rate being 7 per cent. There are still 886,000 people out of work. The government forecast the unemployment rate would average 7.6 per cent over the year. Statistics Canada has said there are 348,000 persons unemployed in the hidden category. This means 1.234 million Canadians are unemployed. The hidden unemployed are those who have given up looking for jobs because they know there are none there for them to find. That is a very serious situation.
Real wages are down for the fourth year in a row. The Economic Council of Canada says they will be down 2.4 per cent this year. We see productivity down for the fourth year in a row. Real growth last year was one tenth of 1 per cent. The forecast this year by the Conference Board, and I will only give one forecast, is that real growth will be 2.9 per cent if strong U.S. growth continues and if work on the oil sands and the Cold Lake projects-the tar sands and heavy oil-resumes by the end of the year. What is the government's response to that situation? It introduced a new energy policy that stopped the Cold Lake and tar sands projects and energy investment in their tracks. I will come to that later.
We must remember, Mr. Speaker, that for every one cent devaluation of the Canadian dollar, about four tenths of 1 per cent is added to the cost of living index in Canada. We must remember that when people say we should not worry about the level of the Canadian dollar. I may be in the opposition, but I am not going to be completely irresponsible as the government was a year and a half ago. For every cent the Canadian dollar goes down, the cost of living in Canada goes up four tenths of 1 per cent because of all the goods we import. We cannot afford to have the Canadian dollar go down much further. It has gone down from $1.02 in 1976 to 83 cents now; a major devaluation. I will come in a few minutes to the reason it is so important that we cannot have our dollar go into a free fall. This would cause chaos in this country, but I will expand on that in a minute.
The Conference Board says that energy investment might reach a 4.5 per cent increase this year compared to 11.4 per cent in 1979 because of the government's new energy policy. Business investment in plant and equipment is now estimated to be 3.6 per cent for this year compared to an average 9 per cent for 1979-80. These are grim economic facts which the government chooses not to deal with. The government wants to ignore them and forget they are there. The government has no policy.
The government's policy in the budget of October 28 was said to be a gradualist approach. The minister says his approach is gradualist, yet he says he supports the Bank of Canada and Mr. Bouey, and so he should. However, in the annual report of the Bank of Canada for 1980 Mr. Bouey said at page 12:
-Canada has made only limited progress since 1975 in containing inflation. The reason is not that the anti-inflationary financial policies followed were miscon-

May 13, 1981

ceived but that they were pursued with such gradualism that they did not succeed in dominating the influences that were working in the opposite direction.
He looked at the last five years and said that our policies have not succeeded. Why have they not? He says they were applied too gradually. The minister says his policies are gradualist policies. This is an admission that his policies are doomed again to failure, as they have failed for the last five years. So much for the minister's approach.
The minister did not have a gradualist approach, the Liberal party did not have a gradualist approach, and members of the government did not have a gradualist approach when they were in opposition in the fall of 1979. No, their approach then was full of guts and gumption. They had the answers. They decried high interest rates, and I will come to that a little later.
The government says it wants to fight inflation, but then the government shows everybody in the country it is not serious because it will not restrain itself. You cannot convince people that you are out to beat inflation if you will not restrain yourself. You cannot ask a worker to restrain his salary demands or the executive to restrain them or the businessman to restrain his profits if the government itself is a big greedy guts colossus that will not restrain its own spending. And spending this year is up. Officially the government says 12.8 per cent, but it is really up about 20 per cent.
The government's budget deficit is $13.7 billion, and this is the tenth in a row. The deficits for the last ten years total $77 billion. Is that a government that shows itself in restraint? How can they ask us to restrain our demands, needs and wishes in Canada to beat inflation when they are acting in this way, when the money is there to burn, a penitentiary here, another expenditure there, all in Liberal districts and for political reasons. There is no restraint whatsoever.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Advertising.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Advertising, and on and on it goes.
The imported oil subsidy is costing $3.8 billion this year. The government has removed it from the estimates to pretend by a piece of fiction that government spending is less than it is. They removed the $3.8 billion cost of the oil subsidy by saying there is a $3.47 billion Canadian ownership account. They are collecting that from the people of Canada through the new petroleum taxes. They are only showing the balance as an expenditure on the oil import subsidy. They show $530 million spent in that way and not $3.8 billion. That is dishonesty in the accounting of the government in the estimates. That is why the government's spending is up 18 per cent to 20 per cent by any true comparison. There is no restraint.
Before the budget came down the Bank of Canada interest rate was 11.76 per cent. The budget came down five months ago. Today the rate is 18.71 per cent, an increase of 7 per cent. That is the result of this minister's budget. That is the result of his gradualism. That is the result of his do-nothingism.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Gradually downward.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
The prime bank rate is 19.5 per cent. I looked at the paper today. Mortgage rates are 18 per cent. The minister says to the people who have homes in Canada, the 500,000 who have to renew their mortgages this year, I think the figure is, "You should not be out spending money; you should restrain your demands if there are high interest rates".
How can you restrain your demand if you have a mortgage for $40,000 on your home, you have to renew it this week and they tell you the rate is 18 per cent? The only way to restrain your demand is to give up your house, to sell your house and live in the poor-house. That is the minister's advice to these hundreds of thousands of Canadians suffering through his and his government's lack of attention over the last ten years. The prime bank rate is 19.5 per cent.
I have a letter from a man in British Columbia. He took out a loan with the federal small business development bank back on December 2, 1980. The rate then was 14.5 per cent. On April 8 he was paying 22.25 per cent. This is the bank which is to help small business. This is what the official government bank was charging on April 8, a month ago, before the recent increases, 22.25 per cent interest on a loan to a small entrepreneur in British Columbia who took it out just a few months earlier, in December, at a rate of 14.5 per cent. That is the government's own bank, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) gets up with his nonsense in the question period about how the private banks are doing this and making profits and they do not consider the farmers. What is the minister's own fat bank doing, the small business development bank? It is charging 22.25 per cent to the small businessman. It has to because it is borrowing money to lend out at rates of 18 per cent, 19 per cent and the rest. That is the way the banking system works. Let him look at the mote in his own eye and not get up with his fat bafflegab about what the banks should be doing, and trying to excuse the government.
The government's economic policy today is to drift, to keep out of view and to hide behind skirts; but the minister is now exposed, and the Canadian people at last are starting to wake up. The constitutional mirage is in the Supreme Court. They are dealing with it, and now we are dealing with the real things that bother people here in Canada, not this constitutional business that is now, luckily, off the political scene for a while.
There is only one area this inactive government has been active in. The new energy policy is their only new creative area, and that has caused the most damage of all. If people want to know why the Canadian dollar is under pressure, why it is in danger and why interest rates have to be stratospheri-cally high to protect the Canadian dollar, it is because of the new energy policy which confiscates 25 per cent of the holdings of the oil and gas industry on federal lands without compensation, which is anti-the private sector, anti-business, anti-American and anti-foreign investment.
That is why funds are not coming into Canada. That is why funds are leaving Canada and depressing the already depressed Canadian dollar. Why is the Canadian dollar already depressed? Because for the last seven years we have had a total of $26 billion in deficits on the balance of pay-
May 13, 1981

ments on our international account. We in Canada are living off the rest of the world. We are borrowing from them. We cannot survive unless they lend or invest in Canada billions of dollars every year to meet these deficits. We are suppliants to the rest of the world. That is why the Canadian dollar is a weak dollar.
The government opposite has been in office for these last ten years, with the exception of a few months, and in those few months they did everything they could to sabotage anyone else who was trying to save the situation. They are afraid to adopt any remedies themselves but gradualism. Well, gradually they have got Canada to the point that the Canadian dollar is one of the orphans of international finance, and Canadian interest rates have to be at 19 per cent, 20 per cent and 21 per cent to get the Americans to send up some short-term money to prop up the Canadian dollar.
This did not happen overnight; it happened over ten or 12 years. There are no quick fixes, no quick solutions. When the press asks, the NDP can give them quick solutions because the NDP has never been in power, will never be in power and lives in fantasy. They have solutions to everything. You wave a magic wand, you freeze prices and you have a commission and all this nonsense. We do not get on with them. We know there are no quick solutions. The minister is bankrupt of solutions. He asks us to give him some suggestions, and I will as I go along, as other members of our party will.
The only active area is the energy policy, and that policy has driven money out of the country, has driven oil rigs out of the country and driven investment out of the country. The government likes to flex its muscles and pretend it is pro-Canadian, anti-American and anti-foreign investment, when really for the last ten years it has been begging the world to lend us money and invest money here. If they do not and if we are not successful, the Canadian dollar will go down the tubes altogether. That is the government's bold policy, the new energy policy.
PetroCan purchases Petrofina; $1.7 billion is the cost to the people of Canada who consume oil and gas. Three and a half cents a gallon was levied on oil and gas and heating products, heating oil, to pay the $1.7 billion required for PetroCan to buy Petrofina, which will not result in Canada having one more cup of gasoline or one more litre or cupful of natural gas. It does not increase the oil and gas assets of Canada at all, and we are paying out $1.7 billion, mostly to people in Belgium. Verily, the patron saint of Belgium must be Mr. Marc Lalonde because he is doing a lot for the Belgians; but he is doing nothing for us. That is another billion dollars depressing the Canadian dollar that has to be paid out over the next two or three years. This is the government's great policy, the only area that they have been active in.
The other damaging area is FIRA. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) is going to supervise all foreign investors in Canada. He is going to amend FIRA. So not only do you now have to pass his scrutiny to invest in Canada, but when you have a business here, he is going to come and look over your shoulder and say, "You are not doing
Interest Rates
the business as I would do the business" or "You are not doing the right thing" or "I don't think this is in Canada's interest". That is the threat. No wonder the Canadian dollar is at 83 cents U.S. I wonder that it can be kept up at all with the likes of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, with his narrow-minded view, with his narrow, parochial Canadian nationalist view, he calls it, threatening how he is going to change the regulations and explaining how he is going to operate.
Then we see the Canada Development Corporation, a government Crown corporation, doing well, operated properly, a major assistance to Canada, with $3.4 billion in assets, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce tries to get them to take over the sick. They say they have a policy of helping the successful, and it turns out to be Chrysler or Massey-Fer-guson and so on. They try to make the CDC take Massey-Fer-guson or Chrysler under its wing when they have 30,000 Canadian shareholders, individuals, small people who invested their money on the promise of the government that that corporation would operate in an ordinary profit-motive manner, concentrating its efforts on developing the resources of Canada. Now we see them attempt to make Maurice Strong, that Liberal candidate who did not even have the fortitude to run after he was nominated, chairman-he started PetroCan-so as to turn this corporation into the new PetroCan in the industrial field, and the hell with the 30,000 Canadian shareholders who were fooled by prospectuses.
Is it any wonder that the investment community lost faith in Canada? It is a wonder that the Canadian dollar is not at 60 cents, much less 83 cents. These are some of the areas where the government has been active.
Just look at interest rates in some other countries. In Germany the central bank rate is 7.5 per cent. The prime bank rate is 12 per cent. France has a 12 per cent central bank rate; Japan, a 6.25 per cent central bank rate; the United States, a 14 per cent and a 4 per cent surcharge for frequent borrowers. Look at the United Kingdom, which these people sneer at and denigrate; they tell them to hold their noses while they send over their dog's breakfast of a Constitution for them to pass. What is the bank rate in England? It is 12 per cent. The inflation rate in England is 12.6 per cent. That is what Mrs. Thatcher has done because she has guts and gumption. She has more you-know-what than all that bunch opposite put together. They have a 12.6 per cent inflation rate.
The U.S. inflation rate is 10.5 per cent; in Japan the inflation rate is 6.2 per cent; in France the inflation rate is 13 per cent; in Germany the inflation rate is 5.6 per cent. This government does not even have the defence that other countries are worse off than we are. The other industrial countries in the world are not. It is just this country, with its sorry, shabby, economically tattered, weary, tatterdemalion government, that is in this kind of shape. It cannot even look to other countries for comfort.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
The Bank of Canada and the minister have admitted that the reason for the present high interest rates is more because of the fear of the Canadian dollar declining if interest rates do not keep up with those in the U.S. That was in the bank's news release of May 7. The minister has said that as well.
1 want the people of Canada to try to understand this. The fault is not with the Bank of Canada. I am talking to the people of Canada because I know hon. members opposite are not listening and will not listen. They will not listen until the people of Canada shake their fists at them, until the people of Canada send them letters, until the people of Canada phone them, until the people of Canada put the pressure on. That is why, through the medium of television, I am speaking to the people of Canada, not to the tatterdemalion remnants across the floor.
The fault is not with the Bank of Canada. It is not with Mr. Bouey. Forget Mr. Bouey; he has done everything he can in his little sphere of monetary operation but he has had no help from the government in the fiscal area in ten years. The government is responsible for Mr. Bouey's interest rates. He recommends; the government decides. It can give him a letter tomorrow saying reduce the rate, do this, do that; and he has to do it. He has done his best for five years. If he had not done what he has, we would be a lot worse off today with respect to inflation than we are. So do not blame Mr. Bouey, people of Canada; blame the Minister of Finance; blame the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). Blame the Prime Minister over all. '

speechtext:
The Prime Minister sits in this House and shrugs. He does not care about interest rates; he does not care about you mortgage holders out there; he does not care about you small businessmen. Why should he? He has lived off you for the last 12 years and he intends to live off you for the next 12. He is so pleased with his success and his unexpected comeback of nine or 12 months ago that he no longer cares. The government should say, like Shakespeare, "the fault is not in Bouey but in ourselves". It is not Mr. Bouey. Forget Mr. Bouey-forgive Mr. Bouey. The Minister of Finance is the only man who can help the Canadian people-if he would adopt the right policy.
What should the government do? The government should start the course it stopped on December 13, 1979. This is my advice to the minister. He should take the approach of the budget of December 11, 1979 and practise real restraint. He should show the Canadian public how the government is going to reduce the deficit over four years; adopt a sensible oil pricing policy-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Never mind; it is my turn to speak. The price has to go up to 75 per cent or 85 per cent over the next couple of years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Don't be so foolish, man; listen and learn!
A sensible energy-pricing policy would give the government the financial relief it needs. It is spending $3.8 billion on a subsidy that should not be spent. It is harmful to the country. That would provide $2 billion or $3 billion with which to assist. Some of that money should be used to help lower income Canadians with an energy tax credit, just as we proposed but which the government stopped. The Canadian people would have had half a billion dollars in their pockets in April if the government had not stopped us. There would have been another one billion, two hundred and fifty million dollars to help the mortgage interest and property tax needs of the householders and mortgagors of Canada, had the government not stopped us. The money is there; it can be done. You can still have restraint and do that.
A true budget, one with real restraint, would show that the government means business. That is why it is needed now. The minister's statement that he is practising restraint, when everything shows that he is not, does not influence anyone. Everyone in Canada today expects that inflation is going to get worse and they are acting accordingly. This itself makes inflation worse.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, start now. That is the immediate thing the government can do. It is a slow process. It took ten years to get Canada into the grim economic shape it is in now, and it is going to take two or three years of proper application of policy and restraint, and of choosing priorities, to get Canada back on a stronger course, to strengthen the Canadian dollar.
What can be done immediately is to reverse the new energy policy; take out the harmful effects of it and retain some of it. Eliminate the anti-foreign investment, anti-private sector, antiprovinces, parts of that policy; make it more attractive to the entrepreneur and the investor. Get an agreement with Alberta now, not tomorrow and not next week but now. Be reasonable. If the government changes its plan and shows it is being reasonable, then the government of Alberta has no choice but to follow suit. So far the government has prevented that from occurring because its proposals are so onerous and so anti-any-thing that the oil producing provinces could accept that there is no chance they could be accepted. I say reverse that situation.
I say to the government, reverse the FIRA nonsense. Leave FIRA as it is. Take Mr. Gray off the backs and the necks and the legs of the people who want to invest in Canada and help the dollar. Reverse the CDC process and let the government show it is not going to break faith with the people who listened to and believed its representations in the prospectuses issued when it sold 51 per cent of the shares of that company to the public.
The inflation rate is going to be 13 per cent at least in 1981 and 1982. These kinds of high interest rates are not needed to deal with that situation; 15 per cent or 16 per cent you might argue, but not 19 per cent or 20 per cent or wherever the rate is going. Come to grips with the situation now.
May 13, 1981

The minister has two choices. Start the process now. You are going to have to inflict some pain. People like to see money spent. We all know how politicians get popular. The Liberal party has been excellent at that; it has been in power since 1963 by these methods. Now the consequences have caught up. You have to start the process now; that is one choice. Start the process now and bring in a new budget that really means something-real restraint, a proper oil pricing policy, an energy tax credit, a shelter allowance, as I have suggested. Drop the FIRA and the CDC nonsense.
If the government continues dithering, continues drifting, Mr. Speaker, then within a number of months less than six it is inevitable that the government will go to wage and price controls. It is going there politically because of the outrage of the Canadian public, which will say "You have to do something to stop this inflation; you have to do something about these interest rates". Because there is no quick and dramatic action that they can take-because they would not start the process months ago and they would not start it a year ago- they will bring in wage and price controls. Not because they think that wage and price controls are the answer. They did not solve anything in Canada permanently five years ago in the three years that they were applied. But that is where the government is heading, to wage and price controls, Mr. Speaker. That is a complete waste of time, Mr. Speaker. It is another extension of state power and interference with the lives of Canadians, another major obstacle and impediment to the market economy that this country is strengthened by because of our resources.
If the government does not act now, it is going to wait for the inevitable and we are going to have wage and price controls or some crazy tax-based incomes policy which the minister's own department says is not the solution. The minister is going to do one of those two things within six months if he does not start the painful process now of straightening out this nation's economy.
I am totally against wage and price controls, but if the minister is going to do nothing now but just dither and continue that policy of 14 months, then I say to him he is better off having wage and price controls brought in tomorrow, rather than waiting until there is an extreme emergency in Canada and bringing them in in the midst of chaos. Is he going to wait for the emergency to arise and then bully and dragoon the provinces into going along with him?
That is the choice. Start the process now, as we started it in December, 1979. They delayed the process. They not only damaged us, they damaged Canada and the Canadian people. They put us years behind, they put the energy industry behind, the tar sands development behind, the heavy oil industry behind. They can start now, or we are going to have wage and price controls.
We need new, revised forecasts. The minister said in his speech on May 6 that interest costs alone last year were up $1 billion more than his budget forecast. We need new, revised forecasts now and he should give them to us in his speech today. Here is the government's borrowing. It cost the govern-
Interest Rates
ment yesterday for a $1.2 billion issue 16.25 per cent in interest. The Government of Canada is borrowing and paying 16.25 per cent interest, and the bonds are selling at a discount. How far have we fallen? The long-term bond market is gone. One must be crazy to invest money in the long term in view of what we see today-the government being afraid to do anything. People are not doing it.
We have had 11 increases in oil, gas and heating oil prices since last year. Only three of them gave anything to the producers; eight of them were tax increases. Gasoline today is 49 cents a gallon more expensive in Montreal than it was a year ago. Heating oil in St. John's, Newfoundland is up 40 cents compared to a year ago. It has gone from 75 cents to $1.15 per gallon; this is over a 50 per cent increase from the minister who promised: "Vote Liberal and the price will stay down". That minister has a lot to answer for. The people voted Liberal, and we know where the price has gone and where it is going.
The minister has a new and callous attitude. He tells the people who have mortgages that it would be wrong for him to give advice as to how to manage their affairs, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen. Also he said that the government would not bail out individuals facing mortgage renewals, and he noted that an analysis last year found most home owners could handle the payments resulting from higher rates. That is what the minister says now. About a year and a half ago he did not say it, nor did his cohorts say it. Now interest rates are 5 per cent higher than they were when gentlemen opposite were in opposition. But today, with four safe years ahead of them, they are saying to Canadians, "You can renew. You have the income. Don't be so foolish. Don't come to us telling us your troubles. You have lots of money to renew. We are not going to give you any help".
That is a callous attitude compared to what they said just a year or a year and a half ago. The seven million home owners in Canada have been kicked by the minister and shown that they will get no relief. Then there are the farmers and the fishermen. Unfortunately I do not have the time to go into all these figures now; I think I am getting near the end of my time. Apparently I only have one minute left.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: You are beyond the end of your rope.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: No, the government is beyond the end of its rope. The people of Canada are beyond the end of their rope.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: If we were not a peaceful, law-abiding country, they would know what to do with the rope. After having somebody tell them, after getting into office on one set of promises-that they are to forget high interest rates and that they have enough income to renew their mortgages-the people of Canada would know what to do with the rope.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Shame.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: They have no shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
There is no shame. I say to the Canadian people right now that we will do what we can in the House. Do not forget, Canadian people, the New Democratic Party helped cause all this. They put us out of office and they put these people opposite back in. They stopped the mortgage interest and property tax credit. They stopped the energy tax credit. They brought on the 19.5 per cent bank rate. They helped the government; they are co-conspirators. They are the rump of the government party, so hold them responsible too.
We in this party heard the Prime Minister say that he would manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would in fact come down, as reported on February 10, 1980.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
As reported in The Toronto Sun on February 4, 1980, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said:
I don't think that allowing the dollar to have some downward adjustment would do as much harm to our economy as our present high level of interest rates.
At that time they were 14 per cent and, as we all know, they are now over 20 per cent.
The minister wants suggestions. It is not our job to run the government. We were put out. Hon. gentlemen opposite had a lot to do with it. We were not politically clever enough. He was more clever then we were politically, but now the minister is the one who is responsible and the chickens are coming home to roost.
My advice to the minister, because he asked for advice, in all due modesty is that he go back and take the approach of the budget of December 11, 1979. The government should make a convincing show that they will restrain themselves; they will still help the needy, those who are the most unfortunate, as we tried to do, but they will restrain themselves after ten years of savage deficits. Give the investors some chance to feel more confident in Canada; make the outside investor feel more welcome. Never mind these other artificial changes in FIRA and the threats which come from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who has never run anything, not even a bull's-eye factory, who says that he will tell the Americans, the Belgians and all the rest how to run their businesses. Forget that, but get together with Alberta in the national interest.
Alberta has had a hard time for the last year since it stopped its negotiations with us and had to go on with this government. They had a pretty severe pummelling; they will be in a more reasonable frame of mind. I am a national politician. I believe in the national government. The agreement must be settled in the national interest.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Alberta is ready to be reasonable, but it is the national government which must change its national energy policy. That will let us strengthen the Canadian dollar. In turn it will allow the Bank of Canada to reduce interest rates. That is the immediate thing the government can do. It should act now. Let us have a settlement of the energy dispute by the end of May and Canadians will get immediate relief. That is my immediate suggestion. I have made more long-term suggestions. The government has put Canada in a position from which it will take a long time to recover. The process must start now. Get some courage and some gumption; they have another four years to go before facing an election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after that scholarly survey of the issue which perhaps can be summarized as, "Do as I did", I would like to put forward some suggestions to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), since he indicated that he is interested in listening to alternatives. We had a debate in December dealing with the critical situation facing the Canadian economy as a result of the interest rate problem, as a result of the severe problem of undercapacity in the economy, as a result of unemployment, as a result of the housing crisis which is facing so many Canadians, as a result of the crisis in bankruptcy which is affecting small business and farmers, the crisis in costs which is affecting fishermen, and the general increases in the cost of food and the cost of living which are affecting every Canadian.
In the last couple of days and in a speech which he made in Toronto last week, the minister made a very similar defence to that which he gave in December. It is the same defence. Although I do not intend to spend any time dealing with the pot-pourri of suggestions which have come forward from the Conservative party, they have ranged today from advocacy of an immediate introduction of wage and price controls to even stiffer cutbacks and harsher economic policies, than are currently being introduced. Apparently even higher interest rates are being suggested in the short term in order to produce magically lower interest rates in the long term.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Don't be such a twister, don't misquote me. I never said that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) has had his turn to speak to the House. I did not interrupt him, even though there were many occasions on which I might have wanted to say something. I would appreciate it if he would give me the same courtesy which I attempted to give him. I will not comment on those policies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have no desire to interrupt the hon. member except when he starts to misquote and put in my mouth words I never said. I did not advocate wage and price controls and I have not said a couple of the other things; I have not suggested higher interest rates. As long as the hon. member quotes me correctly, I have no desire to interrupt him.
May 13, 1981

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. John's West is afraid of the consequences of some of his words. When we read Hansard tomorrow, I am sure we will see exactly what he had to say about wage and price controls. I stand by what I have just described in terms of the effect of what he said.
The purpose of the defence offered today by the Minister of Finance is really twofold. The first is that the interest rate policy which the government is following is necessary in order to support the Canadian dollar. The defence of the Canadian dollar and the relationship between the American and Canadian economies have been the persistent argument which the government and the bank have put forward for many, many years. The secondary defence, which the minister trots out from time to time and has put forward with even greater vigour in the last couple of weeks, is the need to have these kinds of interest rates in order to reduce inflation.
I might remind the minister that this is a significant change from what he was saying in December. If he looks at his remarks in December, he will see that he said that these rates were too high for Canada, but that they were necessary for Canada because of what was going on in the United States.
If I understand him correctly, in the last week he has been saying that these rates are necessary for Canada in order to control inflation, that these rates are not too high or excessive, that in fact they are a necessary part of government strategy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: And they may go higher.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
And they may go higher! He has no idea how high they will go. He is not opposed to the policy being followed by the bank and the effect it is having on the Canadian economy.
I want to say to the minister that what I call the domestic justification for the control of inflation is completely without foundation. There is no economy in the western world among the OECD countries which has real rates of 8 per cent, 10 per cent and 12 per cent as a measure of deliberate policy. Canada is alone in this regard. These are the highest real rates in our history. By any stretch of the imagination they are excessive, even for the objective which the government has set out for the control of inflation. I would ask the minister to come clean on this point: What does he think the real rates should be over time? I want the minister to tell us what rate he really thinks should go to lenders of all different kinds and whether he really thinks a rate of 8 per cent, 10 per cent or 12 per cent is required, even if one accepts the premise that the way to fight inflation is by raising interest rates.
The argument the minister put forward on the foreign exchange justification to the effect that we really have no choice is an argument which does many things. If I may say so, the hon. member for St. John's West did the same thing. He underestimated the real strength of the Canadian economy and the Canadian dollar. If we had an independent interest rate policy I do not think the consequence would be that our dollar would necessarily fall to 60 cents, 65 cents or 70 cents, U.S., as was suggested by the hon. member for St. John's West
Interest Rates
and many other critics who, in my view, have no real faith in the inherent strength of the Canadian economy.
The statement that we have no choice, that we must tie ourselves at every opportunity to the American policy, is an admission of our colonial status. It is an admission that there is no possibility of the government exercising any significant degree of economic independence. It is an admission and a statement that our interest rate policy is not made in Canada in order to respond to the domestic conditions of the Canadian economy but that because of Liberal party policies we have become an economic colony of the United States.
The third approach being taken by the minister, that is, when he talks about wage and price controls and the introduction of a tax-based incomes policy which would have the effect of controlling wages, is one which would create division among the Canadian people. If the minister looks back to the experiences we had under the anti-inflation board, he will see that it limited the ability of the average Canadian worker to keep up with the rate of inflation. It enriched certain Canadians and certain corporations, allowing them to take unfair advantage. It restricted the living standards of the average working person.
The interesting thing about the review released by the minister's department last year was that it showed lower income workers, many of whom work for our largest financial institutions, fell much further behind the increases in the cost of living than did almost all other workers in Canada. The argument put forward from time to time with regard to the 1975 wage controls is that it was an exercise in social justice. It is put forward that it was some kind of incomes policy, which is completely nonsensical. The minister's affection for what he calls, "market forces" and the need to restore what he calls "market discipline" to the economy will result in giving credence to the law of the jungle. The most powerful will receive the biggest increases and the least powerful will receive the smallest, which will simply increase wage disparities. This will increase the sense of unfairness in our society. This will not resolve the fundamental problem of inflation. It will not resolve the escalating prices which we see in so many parts of the economy.
I wish to turn to the alternatives, Mr. Speaker. Basically, the alternatives are fourfold. The first comes under the heading of recognition by the government of the emergency which we are facing. I remind the minister that when the government introduced the anti-inflation legislation in 1975-76 the Supreme Court took cognizance of the fact that there was an urgency and, indeed, an emergency which justified the federal government exercising its ordinary power of control over the economy. The inflation rate at that time was lower than it is today. Indeed, the government was not faced with the out of control situation with which it is faced today. So we need recognition of an emergency.
We need immediate relief-relief for home owners who are caught in a roulette game of time. These are home owners who happen to be renewing their mortgages in one month, who are paying rates two and three percentage points higher than

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
others. Those home owners who renew this year will pay rates four and five points higher than others. Fishermen attempting to buy boats or improve their equipment are facing interest rates which are four to six points higher. Farmers are facing the same absurd situation. We need relief directed to the groups which need it. If we do not have relief we will have not only a reduction of supply-fishermen will fish less and farmers will produce less-but we will face problems of unfairness.
Monetarism represents a kind of roulette, the roulette of not knowing from week to week whether the rate will be up or down. We are creating a nation of speculators. We are making speculators out of the average home owner as a consequence of a policy which needs to be changed. It can be changed through a relief program, under the notion of an economic emergency and urgent situation. For some time we have argued that problems are structural. In a sense, the problems are built into our modern economy. We need a prices commission, not as a temporary measure brought in as a cosmetic device every two or three years but as a permanent feature of the Canadian economy, which will have the capacity to roll back price increases where they cannot be justified.
The provincial governments have a responsibility as well. They have a responsibility to end speculation in housing, to end speculation with regard to farm land. In my view, they have an obligation to encourage land banking and policies which will keep down the price of land for farming and housing. They have a responsibility to see that it is still possible to be able to afford a house in the city of Toronto while making less than $30,000 a year. The minister of housing in the Ontario legislature admitted last week that a person had to make at least $30,000 in order to be able to buy a house in Toronto. That is absurd.
Under the heading of new policies there is quite simply a need to reduce interest rates. There is a need to change the policy. I repeat what I said to the minister: there is no evidence to suggest that any other country is living with rates which are this high and which has no control over those rates. The rates currently being inflicted on the economy are dysfunctional. They do not have the effect of controlling inflation. They have not had the effect of controlling the price explosions which we have seen with regard to housing and, indeed, which we have seen in parts of the food industry. They simply have the effect of contributing to the explosion.
There needs to be a change, a step toward economic independence. There needs to be a determination on the part of the government that Canada's interest rates policy will reflect the domestic condition of the Canadian economy and not the decisions of Congress, the Federal Reserve Board or Wall Street in the United States.
The third heading under which I would suggest to the minister that there needs to be changes is on the tax side. Instead of using the tax system as a way of controlling wages, I have argued many times before in this House and will argue again today that in the context of controlling inflation and of
changing our interest rate policy the government needs to introduce general reforms to bring about fairness in the way it collects revenues and distributes tax burdens. If the government fears an explosion in wage demands because it is failing to deal with inflation and failing to give confidence to the average Canadian worker, it could take positive steps to increase the after tax incomes of working Canadians through a redistribution of the tax levels of different groups in society. That is the meaning of the cost of living tax credit.
The minister rejected the cost of living tax credit out of hand in his speech in Toronto, and I think this shows that he did not really understand it. He said he did not want to give blanket assistance to all groups in society. He said he did not think providing everyone with a set of gloves for dealing with the passage of the hot potato that he was talking about would restore what he calls market discipline.
I say to the minister that the government must give the assurance to the Canadian people, particularly those on low and on fixed incomes, that they, too, are part of Canadian society. They too, must be protected. They must not be left to the vagaries of the market. I cannot believe the minister talks constantly of the "discipline of the market". He knows perfectly well that for many people the market is a jungle; the market is an exercise in systematic unfairness. He knows very well that if we leave people subject to that unfairness they will seek their own private solutions which, in many cases, will be inflationary; they will lose hope and will seek private solutions to public problems. The problem of inflation is not a private problem affecting each individual as if they were Adams in society, but is a problem that affects the whole of society. That is the meaning of tax reform and the cost of living tax credit.
However, there are other things that can be done. We need to have tax reform which will deal with the problem of the banks. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is present. I agree with him. I moved amendments to the Bank Act, 1 say to the Minister of Agriculture, that would have provided the minister with the power to give the assistance to farmers and small businessmen that he was talking about. Those amendments were rejected by the Minister of Finance. It is a pity I did not have his assistance during the summer when we were putting them forward. They were rejected by the Tory opposition who are now speaking so firmly about their commitment to lowering the rates. So we need to have those amendments. We need to have the government introduce tax changes that would put a damper on international speculation. Instead of rejecting out of hand the whole notion of exchange controls and considering them as if they were an undiluted whole that had to be rejected or accepted holus-bolus, I suggest to the minister that he look at changes in the tax system that would discourage international speculation, that would discourage the transfer of hot money from Canada to the United States, and that would give us a greater degree of independence.
If the minister says those suggestions are unacceptable, I remind him that when Governor Bouey appeared before the committee two years ago, when the rates were at 11 per cent,
May 13, 1981

he was asked, "What if the rates go to 15?" He said, "Then we will have to look at alternatives; at that point we will have to start considering alternatives". Well, now the rates are at 20, and the government is still refusing to consider alternatives which would have the effect of dampening speculative demand in the economy of demonstrating to the Canadian public that the government is really serious, and of giving the Canadian people the sense that they have a government which is prepared to respond with measures that are tough and swift, but measures that, above all, are fair.
My concern about the proposals which have been put forward by the minister and which are being put forward by the government now is that they are unfair; and the proposals which are being advocated by the minister as possible changes in the rules of the game, as he puts it, will be even more unfair to the Canadian people.
I therefore move, Mr. Speaker, an amendment to the motion put forward by the hon. member for St. John's West. Seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I move:
That the motion be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the words "unprecedented high levels", the following words:
"for continuing policies that not only inflict hardship on the Canadian people but make Canadian economic independence impossible",-
As a result of this amendment, the motion would read:
That this House condemns the Minister of Finance for permitting interest rates to rise to unprecedented high levels, for continuing policies that not only inflict hardship on the Canadian people but make Canadian economic independence impossible, and calls on the minister to meet his economic responsibilities or resign.
As the debate proceeds over the next few weeks-because this is not a matter which can be discussed intelligently in 20 minutes-we will be putting forward additional policies. I think the minister will see we have attempted to provide for a number of years a coherent critique of what the bank is doing, of what the minister is doing and of what the policy of the government is, to show him that there is an alternative, that it is a credible alternative and not, as has been suggested by the hon. member for St. John's West, a fantasy land alternative. In fact, it is a series of concrete and practical measures which will have benefits for the Canadian people. They are not simply sugar-coated pills that will satisfy everyone. They will deal with the problems of inflation, but will deal with them in a way which is fair and will not bring the Canadian economy to its knees. Neither will they reduce our economic independence or diminish our objective of achieving control by the Canadian people of their own economy, so that the policies of the government will eventually reflect the interest of the Canadian people and not simply respond to conditions which are taking place in the United States.
