speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this particular debate, and I welcome too the speeches which have been made by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae).
I am certain, as they are, that the subject matter of the Canadian economy and the problems it faces will be a matter of discussion in the House of Commons for a good period of time, as it has been since the new Parliament was created. As Your Honour knows, most of the time of the House of Commons since the new Parliament has been in session has been devoted to economic matters, including opposition days and government bills relating to the economy. It is also true that a good deal of time has been focused on the all-important question of the Constitution; but nevertheless, the members of the House of Commons have not neglected discussion of the economy. They have discussed the economy on a number of occasions and on a number of important bills, and they have taken numerous opportunities during question period to examine the government on its economic policies. I hope that trend will continue because the problems that we face, especially on the inflation front, are deep-seated and, as the hon. member for St. John's West has suggested, will not be susceptible to magic, quick or overnight solutions.
As I replied yesterday in answer to a question, the inflationary psychology has become embedded not only in the minds of the public, in the minds of the economic actors in the economy, but also deeply embedded in the institutions and the structures of the economy. It has been built up over a considerable period of time.
I am not ready to engage in a debate about the historic causes of inflation in this country. I do know that in the seventies, when the governments of the provinces and the national government, especially in the early part of the seventies, were strongly pursuing expansionary policies and adding to their deficits, the public and all political parties generally supported that type of fiscal policy. I do know that as successive ministers of finance reduced taxes in the House of Commons over the years in the 1970s, probably in the total amount of $14 billion, their actions were widely applauded and never opposed in the House of Commons.
Notwithstanding that, it may be instructive to review the causes of a good deal of this inflationary psychology. It has been reviewed rather clearly in the annual report of the governor of the bank, which I recommend hon. members read. They may not agree with every part of it, but I think it is a useful survey of the background to the current inflationary situation in the country.
The hon. member for St. John's West has focused his motion on the question of interest rates. I have no complaint with that. Interest rates are high; they are worryingly high.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
They are a manifestation of inflation in the economic environment, and they will not be significantly reduced until the over-all level of inflation is curbed. That is absolutely clear to me.
Since I took on this job there have been three pronounced incidents of interest rate shocks, so to speak. In the spring of 1980 after I became minister, the rates went up and then down again.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: That was the first shock, when you became minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Interest rates have been so volatile that they went up to about 20 per cent in the United States and they came down to 10 per cent, as hon. members will realize, all in the period since March, 1980. Last December they went up to an unprecedented high. They have gone down in the interim, but not as much. They are now up again. Therefore, we have been confronted with volatility in interest rates over that period of time, which have impacted in the United States on the Canadian interest rate situation. No minister of finance could be indifferent to the uncertainty created by the volatility of the interest rate policy pursued in the United States nor could a minister be indifferent to the impact which these changes have had on the Canadian economy.
I want to discuss those external developments, but I do want to say a word about the Canadian economy. The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood drew attention to the fact that in the arguments which I advanced in December-I have not read them but I take his word and they do correspond to my own recollection-the main thrust, or the principal explanation, was pressure from the United States. Indeed, I believe I stated that the Governor of the Bank of Canada had said we were running interest rates in Canada which were higher than those required to control the money supply in this country. As I recollect, if hon. members will go back to the statement made by the governor of the bank during the ministers of finance conference in December, and subsequent to its release, he makes that point apparent.
When I brought down the budget last October, hon. members will recall that I was predicting very weak or negative growth in the economy for 1980.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I cannot listen to this.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I was also predicting a lower inflation rate for 1981 than has subsequently been the case. But that is something quite different. I believe hon. members who are looking at the economy and at what has happened in the economy since last October and last December will have to realize that we are generating considerable inflationary pressures of our own in Canada. We cannot single out pressures from the United States, though they are important, as the sole explanation because there is pressure on rates in our own country.
Hon. members may have noticed that in the statement made by the governor of the bank last Thursday following the very high bank rate announcement the concluding sentence was:
In respect of other economic developments, the bank noted that the rate of total spending and the demand for credit in Canada have both remained disturbingly high.
There is a very strong demand for credit in this country. There is a very strong demand for bank loans. There is a booming real estate market in certain Canadian cities, despite very high mortgage rates at the present time, as was pointed out by the governor of the bank in his speech delivered in Moose Jaw.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Who is buying the homes, Allan?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I have to remind hon. members that in Canada, for example, real output increased at an annual rate of over 8 per cent in the last quarter of 1980. That was quite unexpected. Real output in the first quarter of 1981 ran at annual rates of 4 per cent to 6 per cent. Residential construction in the country was the main area of weakness, especially in the first half of the year. However, the merchandise trade surplus doubled from $4 billion in 1979 to $8 billion. The combined foreign deficit on goods and services fell from $5.8 billion in 1979 to $2.8 billion in 1980. That is on the output side.
I remind hon. members also that in the budget, based upon the projections which had been worked out in the Department of Finance, we projected an unemployment rate of 8.6 per cent, I believe, for 1981. I have not looked up what my predecessor projected, the former minister of finance, but in April of this year unemployment in Canada was at 7 per cent, the lowest unemployment rate we have had in the country since June, 1976.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: You said 8.5 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Either 8.5 per cent or 8.6 per cent. In any event, it is the lowest unemployment rate since 1976.
With respect to employment growth, I gave the figure yesterday. I may have said 360,000 jobs were created but I think it was probably about 346,000 for the same month in 1980, or up 3.3 per cent. This is the employment growth created from April, 1980 to April, 1981. I doubt whether there is any industrialized country in the world with a better employment creation record than Canada had in the last year. Therefore, I do not think hon. members ought to talk about the Canadian economy in stagnation or a Canadian economy which has been unable to create jobs. That is not the case.
There is no doubt that, in addition to the greater strength in real economic activity, not nominal activity, there has been a very disturbing tendency for inflation and inflationary expectations to show signs of deterioration. I have admitted more than once that the outlook for inflation in 1981 is worse than it was at the time of the budget in 1980.
May 13, 1981

The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood talks about a made-in-Canada interest policy. Whatever validity may have existed for that point of view, and I have at times argued against it, I think we are making our own pressure at the present time in the Canadian economy on interest rates. 1 refer hon. members to the comments made by the governor of the bank in his speech in Moose Jaw. He talked about the various forces at work in the Canadian economy, providing reasons for the recent tendency of Canadian interest rates to rise. He went on to say:
Let me recapitulate them: the strength of the current economic rebound in Canada; high and rising inflation and serious fears of still worse inflation to come, a continuing strong demand for credit even with interest rates at levels that normally would have discouraged domestic borrowing; and a persistent weakness of the Canadian dollar that was adding to the upward pressures on costs and prices in Canada.
That is the current situation in the country. The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood may be right in saying that the explanation given last December has to be supplemented.
The second important influence is the pressure we have had on rates from the United States. There is no doubt about it, this second force from the United States has significantly intensified in recent weeks in the very rapid rise in interest rates which have once again occurred in the United States.
Maybe I should say a word about the situation in the United States because it is useful for all of us to know exactly how we see it. The new administration in the United States has taken a strong anti-inflationary stance and regards monetary policy as an important weapon in dealing with inflation. In the longer run, success in reducing the rate of inflation will help lower interest rates, but at this stage it appears that financial markets are focusing more on the possibility that the confrontation of restrictive monetary policy and the inflationary momentum in the economy may be particularly sharp over the next several months, with continuing upward pressure on interest rates.
Whatever one may say about the expectation of the financial markets or the explanation that is mentioned with respect to a conflict between monetary policies and the inflationary momentum within the economy, there is no doubt that we have had, for example, a two percentage point increase in shortterm interest rates over the week, leading to what has happened to the Canadian bank rate.
I ask hon. members, what alternative in these circumstances should the Governor of the Bank of Canada have? Was it a good idea? Up to the present time he has stated, and it is still a legitimate point of view, that when these pressures on the Canadian interest rate situation and the Canadian currency arise from higher interest rates in the United States, one can take some of that pressure in increased interest rates in Canada or a decline in the Canadian currency.
The fact is that Canadian currency at the present time is trading at 83.20. It may be higher. In these economic circumstances, would it be wise to permit a further depreciation in the value of the Canadian currency? A further depreciation in
Interest Rates
the value of the Canadian currency would be inevitable if there were an outflow of capital from this country, not impeded by higher interest rates in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: There is a national outflow when you come to the national energy policy.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I will come to the National Energy Program, if the hon. member wants to talk about it. It is not the problem. It may be part of the solution. I am saying that at the present time, regardless of the National Energy Program, we would have pressures from the United States in the form of very sharp increases in interest rates. How does Canada respond? By a further depreciation in the Canadian currency, a depreciation which would increase the cost to Canadians of all their imported goods, which would bring in a further blast of imported inflation from abroad and would have very little effect on the competitive capacity of Canadian exporters?
There is a great advantage now in terms of the exchange rate given to Canadian exporters. Indeed, it is so great and their incomes are so large that they can afford rather large inflationary wage settlements in the current circumstances. There is no advantage to the Canadian economy, in my view and in the view of the governor of the bank, in further depreciation because it does not give us any competitive advantage and adds to our inflationary problems.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I put a brief question to the minister? I agree with what the minister is saying about the Canadian dollar, but my question to him is this. What policies is he going to adopt and implement to strengthen the Canadian dollar so that we can have lower interest rates and will not need to keep them high to protect a weak Canadian dollar? That is what we want to know. How is he going to do that?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
The hon. member had asked about policies to increase the strength of the Canadian dollar. He will know that the trade figures have been very strong. Indeed, for the past quarter and the quarter before that they have been very strong indeed. They have been contributing to the strength of the Canadian dollar.
The hon. member advocated in the course of his speech and yesterday that a speedy energy agreement with the oil-producing provinces would relieve somewhat the downward pressure on the Canadian dollar and put us in a position where interest rates could come down. I must say that any uncertainty that exists in the economy is best resolved. There is no doubt about that. The Government of Canada has been eager, as the former minister of finance was eager, to secure an agreement with the government of Alberta to relieve that uncertainty in the Canadian economy. Hon. members opposite did not succeed in reaching an agreement and we have not succeeded in reaching an agreement. Undoubtedly when that disagreement is cleared up, it will be better for the Canadian economy. However, I do not see that it will have very much impact on interest rates at the present time.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
If I took the advice of the hon. member for St. John's West I would reach a solution with the government of Alberta which would bring oil prices up to at least 75 per cent of the world level. Indeed, I read the hon. member for St. John's West as having said recently to Alberta: "Hang in there; get your maximum price".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Shame!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: That is what he was quoted as having said: "Hang in there and get your maximum price". If that is his advice to me, I want to tell him that conceding to Alberta's price demands would have a very big impact on the inflation situation in Canada. Would acceding to their pricing agreement help inflation very much?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: It certainly would have a pronounced effect on the CPI, and that is why I was rebuking the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) yesterday, who was complaining about increases in the CPI, when she supported a motion at her convention that would immediately increase the price of energy to 75 per cent of world prices.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I certainly do not wish to interrupt the minister just because he refers to me, but when he makes a statement about me that is totally incorrect, I do feel I have to draw his attention to the fact that what he says is not at all correct. There was no such thing as a resolution passed at our convention which said that the price of oil should go to 75 per cent of world prices immediately. That simply is not true and the minister should not be allowed to make these false statements.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not attend the Conservative convention, but I did read press reports which stated quite clearly that the member from Etobicoke had argued against a proposal made by the Alberta Conservatives that the oil price should go up to 85 per cent of the world level, and that he had succeeded, because of the political dynamite behind the proposal, to get his supporters in the hall to agree to 75 per cent of world prices. That was the press report.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: A point of order, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Order, please. Whether it be the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) or any other member who has the floor, the Chair has no choice but to recognize an hon. member who stands on a point of order and at least hear the beginning of his comments to determine whether in fact there is a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was at the convention, and the Alberta delegates did not argue the way the hon. minister just
said. He should not be talking on spec; why not get some facts?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Why don't you come to one of the conventions and find out what goes on?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: What are you going to gain by saying these things that are untrue?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have to go to the Conservative convention, nor do I have to read the press reports, because members are rejecting all that has been attributed to them in the press, namely, that they support 75 per cent of world prices.
The hon. member for St. John's West was quoted recently as telling Albertans when he was in the west to hang in there on their pricing agreement; he was telling Alberta to hang in there. 1 am telling him that the year over year increase in the consumer price index would jump to 16 per cent. That is what would happen. For the year as a whole-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hon. members opposite find this very difficult to take. I listened very carefully and intently to all the comments by the hon. member for St. John's West and he is doing the same thing. He is not protesting about the statement attributed to him in Alberta when he said: "Hang in there Alberta and get what you want". That would represent an increase in the cost of living to 16 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I want to tell hon. members that the price agreement which they allegedly brought about called for an increase in prices within a four-year term to 75 per cent, and then 85 per cent of world prices. Do they still stand for that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Get the facts.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Do they still stand for that increase in the CPI? Do they believe that if that is brought about, these increased energy prices would not filter through to the rest of the economy? Will they not concede in those circumstances that in order to restrain the inflation which would be caused by these very substantial energy price increases embedded in the CPI, we would require a very tight fiscal and monetary policy? In my view, an immediate energy settlement along the lines proposed by the hon. member for St. John's West would not have much of an impact on the current high interest rates we are facing in this country. In fact, the hon. member said to me to get an energy agreement with Alberta, but not at any price.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: We don't want it at any price.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I am telling hon. members opposite that when they make these pricing proposals, they ought to relate them to their concerns about the cost of living and interest

rates, because in both cases they will hurt and not help. I want to remind hon. members about that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: When?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: -as early and as quickly as possible, but it will be an agreement that will preserve the interests of all Canadians. It will not be my intention to ransom the future of Canada because of the current high interest rates we are facing in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Your deficits are already doing that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Albertans are Canadians and you should remember that.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Of course Albertans are Canadians, and no one would think of making that comment except the hon. member himself. I certainly would not make it or imply it in any way.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: When I talk about the interests of all Canadians, I am speaking of the interests of the province of Alberta as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Give them a fair deal.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I agree with all hon. members that an early energy agreement with Alberta would be desirable, but it will require accommodation on the part of the province of Alberta as well as accommodation on the part of the Government of Canada. It will require a constructive compromise between the two governments. As I have said on earlier occasions, it is not a matter of capitulation or surrender on the part of either side because neither side will do that. There will have to be compromise, adjustment and accommodation on both sides, and that is what we are seeking at the present time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: For how long?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES

To follow the hon. member's suggestion of going to the price levels he is advocating at the present time, I say, would be even more inflationary than any of the other proposals which were in his budget.
Interest Rates

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I know I am coming to the end of my time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: You sure are.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I regret that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands should be so raucous during the course of debate. She has constantly interrupted me from her seat, which is something I never do, and I hope she will stop it so that I can use my time more profitably.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Be serious.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I just want to make the contrast. The advice given by the hon. member for St. John's West to me was to "bring back my budget". That was his advice. He said, "We had expenditure restraint in the budget". I believe in expenditure restraint because in the expenditure line which I have projected for the next several years there is a clear commitment to expenditure growth within the growth rate of the gross national product and to bringing about from year to year a decrease in the rate of growth of public spending. We are committed to expenditure restraint, but I asked my friend, the hon. member for St. John's West, if he really believes in expenditure restraint, why he does not convince the other members of his party about expenditure restraint so that every day we will not be faced with a barrage of requests from hon. members opposite to introduce new spending programs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: That is not true, and you know it.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: The most notable example was the view expressed yesterday by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands who seemed to be saying to me that I must take special action to protect every particular group in the country. I believe in expenditure restraint, I believe in bringing down inflation, and I believe that in order to bring down interest rates we have to bring down inflation, but we will not bring down inflation if I respond to every request made in the House of Commons for additional spending by adding to the deficit, adding to our financial requirements and putting further pressure on inflation in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) was saying. I did not want to interrupt him, but I wonder if he would entertain a question.

Agreed.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has said on numerous occasions in the House that interest rates in Canada are subject to influences beyond the control of the government. I understand in part what he is saying. If interest rates in Canada are lower than they are in the United States or elsewhere, then money will flow out of our country, and that would have a dramatic effect on our dollar. In part, at least, interest rates must be kept up because of this.
Just recently Premier Lougheed of Alberta made a suggestion to the Minister of Finance and the federal government in general. He said that if they would remove the export tax on natural gas and allow more gas to be exported from Alberta, that would go a long way toward solving the federal government's problem and would allow it perhaps then to decide whether it could reduce interest rates. In fact, he suggested that if the federal government would allow more exports of gas, that would certainly help reduce interest rates in Canada.
Does the minister agree with that statement by the Premier of Alberta, and would he consider taking that action?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to enter into the debate on the important subject of interest rates, but before I do, I wish to note, as the House realizes, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) was rushed, and because of that he did not refer in his comments to the fact that of the 11 energy price increases since he took office, eight were the result of tax measures imposed by the Minister of Finance on the Canadian people. I know the minister would want that on the record.
We heard a great number of statistics about international finance from the Minister of Finance. I would like to spend some time this afternoon talking about people because the Canadian people are faced with the monetary policies of the Bank of Canada which decree high interest rates to support the Canadian dollar and to control inflation and a federal government which completely ignores the plight of Canadian home owners, farmers and small business. As a result, the current prime interest rate at Canadian banks is 19.5 per cent. But home owners, farmers and small businessmen do not pay at the prime rate. They are paying over 20 per cent. These people, the backbone of Canada, are being crushed by the indifference of the Liberal government.
In the fall of 1979, the hon. member for Windsor West, who is now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), speaking on behalf of the Liberal party, made some comments to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs about the prime rate at that time. He said it would mean the loss of thousands of jobs, it would mean increases in the cost of living, it would put housing beyond the reach of middle and lower-income Canadians, it would hurt small business which depends upon bank borrowing to operate, and it would hurt farmers who have the same dependence on bank borrowing and therefore add to the cost of food. One does not normally rush to support the comments of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, but these comments were surprisingly accurate. However, if that particular member was upset at that time when he was a member of the official opposition, where is he now as Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce? When he made those comments, the prime bank rate was 14 per cent. One would think he would be beside himself today because of the lack of action on the part of the Minister of Finance when the prime rate is 19.5 per cent. However, he has sat in the House for the past two days smug and satisfied and without a flicker of concern as we on this side of the House have expressed our concerns on behalf of the Canadian people and Canadian industry and commerce.
The high interest rate policy of the Liberals has created chaos in the housing market. On the one hand there are signs of consumer panic in some major metropolitan centres. Supply has contracted, but demand has soared as Canadians strive to own homes. The minister responsible for housing recently stated that a large percentage of Canadians do not prefer home ownership as their style of living. That is nonsense. The
May 13, 1981

1976 census showed that 62 per cent of Canadian households were owner-occupied. Many tenants want to own a home. Canadians are buying homes at an unprecedented pace. Canadians are afraid that mortgage interest rates and prices will soar even higher. And why not? They do not see any definite action on the part of the Liberal government to alleviate the problem. Therefore, they are buying homes at inflated prices and paying absurd interest rates to carry them because they are afraid that soon they will be out of their reach.
At the same time, there is the tragedy that many Canadians are selling their homes, not because they do not want to own a home but because they just cannot afford to carry the one they presently own, or they see a mortgage renewal at prohibitive rates in the near future.
Home owners who purchased homes with 10 per cent mortgages five years ago are faced with 18 per cent mortgages today. It costs $360 to amortize $40,000 at 10 per cent over 25 years and $590 to amortize $40,000 at 18 per cent over 25 years. That increase of 61 per cent is pretty hard for the average Canadian family to find. So those home owners, discouraged and defeated by the Liberal party's high interest rate policy, are retreating to the status of tenant.
A real estate agent friend of mine in Orillia has suggested that there may not be all that much comfort for them as tenants. When the present mortgage financing of 10 per cent and 11 per cent on rental housing expires, those mortgages will be refinanced at the Liberal rate of 18 per cent. The cost of rental housing is sure to rise in the near future. Many Canadians, unable to sell their homes, are simply walking away from them.
Last year, thousands of Canadians, enrolled in the first year of the AHOP program in 1975, abandoned their homes when the five-year mortgages came up for renewal. This year, the number will increase dramatically because of increased interest rates and the fact that 1976 was the biggest year for the AHOP program. We have suggested that the minister responsible for housing study this problem and beat it to the punch, and so help Canadians to keep their homes, but to no avail.
The minister responsible for housing reported that at a meeting of representatives of banks and trust companies, he was told that the number of foreclosures was down. We can only hope that the minister was wise to their game.
There are two methods by which mortgagees can act to enforce their security upon default: foreclosure and power of sale. Foreclosure is history. Power of sale is now the popular method in Ontario. Fifteen days after default, trigger-happy banks and trust companies are starting power of sale proceedings.
In 1980 CMHC lost $231 million on the sale of repossessed real estate. Despite the comments today of the minister responsible for housing, we are all shocked at the $10,000 per unit loss and the human tragedy that is involved in those repossessions.
Interest Rates
The chaos created by the Liberal party's high interest rate policy has swept away the traditional stability of five-year mortgages. Up until the mid-1960s, some life insurance companies were still lending out mortgage money with 25-year terms. The amortization rate and the term were equal. During the years 1965 to 1979, the five-year term became standard. Now mortgages are renewed for one and two years. There is even talk of a six-month term. Certainty for five years has been replaced with one and two-year uncertainty. Canadian home owners and the Canadian mortgage market have lost stability under the term of the Minister of Finance.
Despite the hardships faced by Canadian home owners, the only action taken by the minister responsible for housing is to continue to reiterate his refusal to act. That is not action. This House does not know the reasons for the minister's apparent lack of concern. It may be his conviction that a large percentage of Canadians do not prefer home ownership as a style of living. This is a conviction which is not shared by members of the Progressive Conservative party or the public. He may be hesitant to act because the minister of housing was the only one of 11 ministries in the social development envelope that had its budget slashed. It may be that the minister is simply embarrassed by having had to reverse previous statements on the community services contribution program, shelter allowances and rent controls.
In any event this House will know that the Progressive Conservative party introduced legislation which would have assisted Canadian home owners faced with today's horrendous mortgage interest rates. Our mortgage interest and tax credit legislation would have met almost one half of the increase in mortgage interest caused by the Liberal party's high interest rate policy. But the Liberal party and the NDP voted against mortgage interest relief for Canadian home owners.
I wish to move on to comment briefly upon the effect of the Liberal party's high interest rate policy on farmers. High interest rates are driving established farmers out of business, making it difficult for young farmers to get started, and will eventually result in higher food prices. Farmers borrow money for seed fertilizer, feed and farm equipment. The cost of borrowing that money and the cost of supplies purchased has escalated. As a result, a well-respected established farmer from Mara Township in my riding, recently told me that last year his expenses had doubled but his income was only a shade higher than the previous year.
How are younger farmers to survive? If farmers have higher expenses, they must, quite properly, increase the price of the food they produce. This increases the cost to consumers. I ask the Minister of Finance how that helps to fight inflation?
A farm implement dealer outside of Orillia recently suggested that if something is not done about the Liberal party's high interest rate policy, there will soon be no inventory left in the country. The average gross margin on all performance implement dealers in Canada was 6.9 per cent last year. That does not leave enough margin to carry inventory over until next year. Farmers cannot afford to buy the equipment and implement dealers cannot afford to carry it.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
Is it not typical that, while the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce seeks to rescue Massey-Ferguson, the Minister of Finance makes it impossible for Canadian farmers to buy the product?
While the Minister of Finance ignores the problem, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has not been idle. His contribution was to increase the interest rate on farm credit loans from 12.75 per cent to 14 per cent effective April 1, 1981. With friends like that, does the Canadian farmer need enemies?
The third group which is suffering from the Liberal party's high interest rate policy is small business. On Thursday of last week, I was contacted by a tourist operator in my riding with a familiar plea: Did I know of any relief for small business from today's high interest rates? She and her husband had purchased the business three or four years ago. They had worked hard together to build up their business and they were just beginning to see the results of their efforts. Unfortunately, their first mortgage was coming up for renewal in June. They had been paying 10 per cent, but now the mortgagee was demanding prime rate plus 1 per cent, or over 20 per cent. This would result in an increase of over 100 per cent in mortgage interest payments alone, and add over $30,000 to their outlay each year. She and her husband were at their wit's end. They would be forced to put their business up for sale or face losing their equity on a foreclosure.
That example is being repeated across Canada. The spirit of initiative, hard work and pride of ownership are being driven out at a time when those qualities should be protected and encouraged. Small businesses across Canada are being driven into bankruptcy through no fault of their own.
Canadian businesses have traditionally used bank financing on a permanent, semi-permanent or cyclical basis. The cost of borrowing money has been budgeted at reasonable interest rates and incorporated into fiscal planning. But now business is faced with the disastrous fiscal policy of this government which disrupts all planning.
Bureaucrats and Liberal politicians who have never had to meet a payroll are creating chaos. Business people who have worked hard, did not go to Hawaii, like the Minister of Finance, and cut every possible corner, now find their expenses escalating because of this government. Business will be forced to increase prices in order to survive. The Liberal party's high interest rate policy does not fight inflation; it fuels inflation and causes bankruptcy. The Governor of the Bank of Canada has stated that the Bank of Canada cannot fight inflation alone. Well, it is not doing so. It has provided absolutely no innovation and no policy.
Home owners, farmers and small businesses are fighting inflation and trying to cope with high interest rates. They are the army. As usual, the Liberal party has not even signed up for the draft. The battle is not being fought on the beaches of Jamaica and Hawaii where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance, both well-known warriors, have spent most of their recess while the rest of us were in our ridings listening to the complaints of little people, Canadian
people. We were not on those beaches; we were in our ridings. The battle is being fought in Canada by little people, not on the beaches of Jamaica and Hawaii.
OO)
The Minister of Finance has not been silent on the issue; he has been very forthright. In fact, after a lifetime of circumlocution, the Minister of Finance has looked inflation full in the eye and stated with finality:
I am not going to begin to advise individuals on how they ought to conduct their personal affairs. I think that would be presumptuous.
He is correct. Indeed it would be presumptuous for anyone earning $66,700 a year, tired from the rigours of a flight back from Hawaii, to advise us common folk on how to conduct our affairs.
What can the minister tell Canadians about the costs of raising a family, making mortgage payments, meeting a payroll and raising a crop? Nothing. It would be more than presumptuous; it would be downright ridiculous. The Minister of Finance makes the captain of the Titanic look inventive.
The other spectators at the battlefront are the Canadian chartered banks. With all the personnel, with all the economists, M.As and Ph.Ds at their disposal, they have failed the Canadian people in their hour of need. How keen are the banks to put out money on small business development bonds? Are they as keen as they were under the Small Businesses Loans Act? I hope not. Are they using switch and bait techniques to go to conventional loans? Why has the average spread between what the banks pay out on savings deposits, as opposed to the prime rate they charge, increased from 2 per cent in the first two months of 1980 to 3.82 per cent in the first two months of 1981? Who is watching over that on the other side? Why are commercial mortgages almost impossible to get? They do not even look favourably on renewals. Why has the word come down from head office to get appraisals on fixed assets involved in loans to businesses connected with farming? Why are they closing down branches in towns and small villages? Why have bank profits increased dramatically? When will we see some initiative and innovation from Canadian banks? Canada may not have had a bank failure since the Home Bank in the 1920s, but I suggest that Canadian banks are morally failing Canadians every day as they face this crisis.
Our current problems are the direct result of a government which lacks the moral fibre to tackle the problem, led by a leader whose main concern is writing a political epitaph. An uninterrupted string of deficits has caused the federal government to escalate its borrowing; 16.7 per cent of the federal budget expenditure is committed to repaying interest on the government's borrowing, to say nothing of principal. The Minister of Finance blithely predicted a deficit of $13.7 billion in October, based on an inflation rate of 10.2 per cent. Since that time, he has admitted in speeches that inflation is running at 13.9 per cent. If the Liberal government were prepared to make a commitment to living within its means, perhaps we would see an end to escalating deficits which would strengthen
May 13, 1981

the dollar. In addition, a commitment by the government would stimulate action by Canadian people.
At present we have anticipatory inflation in Canada; people anticipate that inflation will continue at rampant rates. They govern their wage demands and buying patterns accordingly. They escalate their wage demands because they know they will need more to buy food, clothing and shelter. They buy on credit because they know they will be paying with cheaper dollars. Another positive step the government could take would be to settle the national energy crisis as soon as possible. It would lead to increased production, guarantee security of supply and, eventually, a reduction in the deficit.
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that Canada is experiencing difficult times as a result of the lack of action by the Liberal government to integrate legislative action with its high interest rate policy. Home owners, farmers and small businesses are fighting the battle against inflation with absolutely no help from the government. We call on the government to take action on behalf of Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will have another opposition day, at which time we will look at interest rates as well as some broader factors such as inflation, the growth of the economy and the general government economic policy. Today I would like to restrict my comments to a fundamental analysis of the interest rate situation with which we find ourselves faced today in order to help others understand precisely the causes of that problem and the necessary steps which must be taken by the government. In fact, those steps are being taken.
My interest is not so much in an historic review of why we are where we are, but it is what must be done to resolve the problem with which we are faced. If interest rates are to be reduced, there must be a reduction in the rate of inflation. There are several contributing factors to today's high interest rates, and primary among those is the unacceptable high rate of inflation. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated in his speech in Toronto on May 6, inflation in Canada is not only high but it is growing, that expectations are increasing, that we are seeing an alarmingly high rate of inflation which is rising in an alarming way.
Also he indicated in that speech that the inflation rate for the 12 months prior to October, 1980, was 10.9 per cent. For the five-month period since October, inflation has in fact increased at a rate of some 13.9 per cent. This is the fundamental underlying cause of the high interest rates with which we find ourselves faced. It must be reduced if we are ever to see interest rates at low levels once again.
The second fundamental factor involved in this high interest rate condition is the transition through which we are going toward a more appropriate monetary policy for a lower inflation rate in the future. The transition is a combination of a reduction in the growth rate in the money supply, which is being most appropriately followed by the Governor of the
Interest Rates
Bank of Canada and on the other side, the rising inflationary expectations on the part of the public. The effect of those two factors is that we are finding a reduction in the real lending funds as a result of the reduced growth rate in the money supply. Now we have target ranges from 4 per cent to 8 per cent, coupled with an increase in demand for credit on the other side. With a reducing supply in real terms, and an increase in demand, there are upward pressures on the real rates of interest which are found in the marketplace. As the minister and others indicated earlier, our targets for the increase in money supply in 1981 are 4 per cent to 8 per cent, while demand for credit in April alone increased by 20 per cent.
The third factor which contributes to the present interest rate condition is the external interest rate pressures being imposed on Canada and other nations of the world from the United States. It is a contributing factor; I do not think it is the fundamental factor. The fundamental factor is inflation. Another major factor is the transition toward lower growth rates in the money supply in our anti-inflation policy, and the third factor is the interest rate pressures from the United States. All things being equal, certainly rising rates in the United States will lead to an outflow of funds from Canada to the United States for people to take advantage of the available higher rates of return on money. Short-term money can move across boundaries very easily. In fact, it does move across boundaries very easily. As the minister pointed out, and as the governor of the bank has pointed out, we can take this pressure which we face from short-term capital flowing in and out of the country either through a reduction in the value of our currency as money flows out, causing an imbalance in our current account, or by allowing our interest rates to rise. The governor of the bank and the Minister of Finance have, in my mind, appropriately chosen to take some of the pressure on the dollar and some of the pressure on rising interest rates.
Let me reiterate the third factor, namely, the U.S. interest rate factor. It is but one of the factors contributing to the high interest rates we now face, but it is certainly an important one. It is important to understand that the government and the minister are firmly and unequivocally committed to reducing the rate of inflation in this country. This can be seen if one reads the speech given by the minister last May 6 to the Conference Board of Canada in Toronto. To me this is a fundamentally important policy decision which the government has taken. It is one the government has had to take. It is one that all members of this House and all members of society should support. The reason I believe that this policy is so fundamentally important to the country is not only that inflation has certain obvious ramifications for our society which we all see, but, from a longer term perspective, there are much more deep-rooted, fundamental problems which arise in a society in which chronic inflation is increasing over time. We can see the obvious damage being done to farmers, small businessmen and consumers in the form of general consumer credit. Obviously, these are the damaging effects of inflation.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
These problems are the fundamental reason why the government must undertake, and has undertaken, an effective antiinflation policy, and why that policy must be adhered to, and why we must not back down in the face of adversity. More important, these problems have an effect on the moral fibre of the nation and on the very nature of democracy itself. I firmly believe that. Other scholars who have looked at the historical effects of inflation have come to the conclusion that inflation is a socially debilitating disease which, once it becomes entrenched and if it is not attacked by the powers which can reduce it, causes society to come apart at the seams. I think hon. members will agree with that. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) referred to this concept in his speech.
It is useful to look at the 1950s and 1960s versus the 1970s, when inflation began to get out of control. If we compare what our society was like in the 1950s and 1960s, when we had low rates of inflation, with what it was in the 1970s, and then compare those figures with those in any number of nations-I think of Latin America where there are high rates of inflation and the Weimar Republic in Germany in the 1920s-we find that low inflation societies tend to have high degrees of individual freedom. There tends to be social mobility in those societies. There tends to be a belief in opportunity through hard work, ambition and all of the values on which Canadian society has been built. In those societies people believe in the system; they have confidence in the future. If we look at a high inflation society, we find that the values of honesty, industry and saving tend to lose their virtue. We find there is no perceived assurance that the future can or will be better than it is today.
I think we are beginning to see that kind of attitude emerging in Canada today. It is an attitude which worries me greatly. When we talk to our constituents, we find among them the attitude that the future will not be as good as it is today, or at least it will not be any better. That is a cause for worry in our society. People ask themselves why they should save when the value of their savings made today will be less than what they put down in real terms. People ask themselves why they should invest when the future is increasingly uncertain. If it has one debilitating effect on society and our economic system, inflation increases uncertainty dramatically. We find people beginning to put their money in other stores of value, such as gold or real estate, and not into productive investment which leads to an increase in the wealth of society. We find there is a growing demand for government to intervene, to protect and provide that assurance which the system no longer seems to be able to provide on its own. That assurance is being taken away as a result of inflation.
Let me say in summing it up that you find people undertake a live-for-today policy. They say, "Why worry about tomorrow when tomorrow will not be as good as today? Let us live for today, let us spend today, let us not save or invest, let us not try to make things better for future generations, since future generations will have to face a much worse world than what we face." When that kind of philosophy takes hold in the
system, the democratic way of life cannot long stand and tolerate it.
That is why it is critically important for the government to move forward expeditiously and effectively in an anti-inflation program. In the transition period we will all have to adjust. The government will have to adjust as well as the individual. I will show tomorrow that the government is making that adjustment and that it is committed to making it. I will show tomorrow, when we talk about the budget and its fundamental factors, what the thrust of the budget is.
These are the reasons why the government is solidly committed to anti-inflation measures. In the minister's speech to the Conference Board in Toronto, he said:
The Government of Canada will allow nothing to take precedence over its commitment and efforts to reduce inflation over the medium term.
The minister could not have put it in more firm or unequivocal terms.
I would like to relate these comments on inflation back to the topic which is before us today in the opposition motion which specifically deals with interest rates. I wish to consider the relationship between inflation and interest rates. There is mass confusion going on in our society these days, as well as in this House from certain members, that interest rates cause inflation and therefore we must do everything possible to reduce them. Nothing could be further from the truth. Interest rates do not cause inflation; inflation causes interest rates. We must undertake fundamental policies which attack the root causes of high interest rates. The root causes are high rates of inflation. Interest rates are a function of inflation, just as a fever is a function of an illness, and not the other way around. Inflation is everywhere, it is a monetary phenomenon. I think the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance realize this clearly. That is why the governor has undertaken the policy of reducing the growth rate in the money supply over time. Some hon. members may ask why the governor undertook this policy on a gradual basis, and I will refer to that in a couple of minutes.
The cause of inflation is excessively rapid increases in the money supply relative to growth in real output, or GNP. That is the fundamental cause of inflation. That is what must be attacked if we are to be successful.
The ramifications of such policies will lead to transition effects, one of which will be higher interest rates. The Bank of Canada is committed not to accommodating increases in the money supply or to use increases in the money supply to accommodate increases in relative prices; relative prices of energy, for example, or relative prices of other basic commodities. There has to be adjustment, there has to be substitution, and there has to be conservation in response to higher relative prices of goods and services, even though they are very fundamental.
The reason the governor and the government have undertaken a policy of gradualism on the monetary side and gradualism on the energy side is that the kinds of adjustments and
May 13, 1981

transitions which must take place in our society in response to rising relative prices of food and energy are difficult. They require capital investment by individuals. They take time to accomplish. If the government did not undertake a policy of transition to allow the individuals in our society the time to make those adjustments, then the disastrous effects would be great. The government has undertaken a policy of gradualism to allow that period of transition and for individuals to make those adjustments as painlessly as possible. That is why we follow a policy of gradualism. So with this as background on the current interest rate situation, as I have indicated, we have an inflation rate which has grown over the last five months. Right now it is a rate of 13.9 per cent.

The people have to realize that there is an anti-inflation program that is going to be effective, that the inflation rate is going to come down, and that interest rates will be brought down in its wake.

speechtext:
If we look at just the inflation factor at 13.9 per cent, that implies that to get a zero real rate of return, savers, those people who are saving for retirement or a home or for some future consumption purpose, will have to get an interest rate of at least 14 per cent just to break even. No one in our society should expect savers to subsidize borrowers, to take less than 14 per cent if that is the expected inflation rate. No one should expect our savers to take less than the real rate of return. As a result, we have to expect that they will demand higher than 14 per cent on their money.
How much higher? If we look at the situation back in the fifties when the effective rate of inflation was sometimes very close to zero, and ask ourselves what the mortgage rate was when inflation was next to zero-the mortgage rates then ran between 4 per cent and 5 per cent-and if we look at the current rate of inflation and add to that the mortgage rate, which was the rate when there was no inflation, of 4 per cent to 5 per cent, we find mortgage rates of 18 per cent to 19 per cent.
That is unacceptable. It is unacceptable to all of us. But the fact of the matter is that when we couple the inflation reality with the transition effects which I mentioned earlier and, at the same time, the U.S. situation, we find that those factors
Interest Rates
are putting rates where they are now. Fundamentally, the only way we will see rates come down is to solve the inflation problem. If the inflation problem is basically monetary, it means that we must bring down the growth rate in our money supply to bring inflation under control. The transition period will require interest rates which are higher than we would expect, higher than normal, and higher than we would like to see.
However, I will tell Your Honour-and I firmly believe this to be the fact-that if we renege now on the policy of anti-inflation, if we renege now on the Bank of Canada policy, if we increase the money supply, in the-
