-unfounded effort or belief that by expanding the money supply interest rates will come down, we will feel inflation, and we will have a worse situation six months down the road. We will truly have an inflationary situation in this country which is out of control and we will be facing interest rates which will make today's rates look low by comparison.
The government has a policy. That policy will be effective. I encourage and urge the government to stick to that policy and to see that in the future Canadians face lower inflation and much lower interest rates.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome this occasion to join in the debate today on behalf of the motion put forward by my colleague the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). In doing so, I would doubt very much that we have ever faced a more serious situation over the past number of years than we have here today with reference to the government's inability to deal effectively with the economy. We have record deficits, we have record inflation rates, and we have crippling interest rate levels.
Certainly we have had our share of problems over the years in all sectors of our economy. I suppose most people would agree that the agricultural industry has been no exception. In fact, that industry has probably received a greater share of problems in comparison with other sectors of the economy. I am sure that all would agree that we will continue to have these problems in certain commodity areas and in various provinces and regions of the country in the future.
In all seriousness, I can think of no other single problem that is so damaging and so devastating to all of the food producers of Canada, regardless of their location or lines of production, than the present interest rate level. One can think of the fruit producer in British Columbia; one can think of the problems experienced by the grain and livestock producers of western Canada in the prairies; one can think of the problems associated with high interest rate levels as they relate to the dairy farmers in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; or one can consider the serious problems which face the diversified agricultural industry in Altantic Canada.
However, it is not my purpose today, nor is it really my nature, to promote more anxiety and to promote more fear or

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
perhaps more anger than already exists in this country today as it relates to this government's deliberate high interest rate policy and the continuing high interest rate level which flows as a direct result. Rather, I want to give a few examples of how this serious problem affects the industry and some suggestions to at least provide some relief.
We have to acknowledge the fact that in 1980 Canadian farmers paid $1.5 billion on interest rate charges alone. Agriculture Canada, which is, speaking from my experience, a pretty good source of information, estimated that in 1981 the Canadian farmers will pay at least $2 billion on interest rate charges alone. A bank interest rate of 18.71 per cent and a prime rate of almost 20 per cent are crippling and are absolutely unacceptable levels. They have caused a crisis situation in the agricultural community.
The deliberate high interest policies of the federal government have forced many farmers into bankruptcy or near bankruptcy. For example, on last Monday evening, the CBC news profiled the Gershbakker Brothers of Saskatchewan. They had a $2 million livestock operation, yet they are barely able to scrape together enough cash to meet day to day expenses. Why? One of the basic reasons is the fact that their interest rate charges alone amount to some $43,000.
Again, in the April 15 edition of The Globe and Mail there is an account of a 24-year-old farmer from the province of Ontario, Glen Smith, being interviewed. He said, "Last month the bank gave me one day's notice to pay off $170,000. When I couldn't raise the money, they sent in the trucks, took away the livestock, and they left me with nothing. The farm is frozen today, and I can't even plant a crop this season."
Another Ontario farmer, Don Morrison, was quoted as saying, "I am selling to a businessman in Australia and then I am going to rent the farm back. I don't like it but I have no choice. With inflation and interest rates the way they are-I paid some $30,000 in interest rates last year-selling my land and renting it back is the only way I can keep on farming and possibly make a profit."
Cold statistics add substance to these personal stories. In Ontario, farm bankruptcies increased by 91 per cent last year, compared to an 18 per cent increase for other businesses. The Ontario Federation of Agriculture has estimated the number of bank foreclosures or the number of farmers who have sold out because they were losing money. These numbers are at least ten time higher than the number of bankruptcies in the province.
Other telling facts have been provided by the Farm Credit Corporation. As of March 31, 1981, the number of Farm Credit Corporation accounts or farm operations in arrears ranges from an incredible 33.3 per cent in Newfoundland to 6 per cent in Saskatchewan and British Columbia. In Manitoba there were some 409 farm operations in arrears in 1980, while in 1981, this figure increased by almost 200 to a total of 606 farm operations in arrears, on their loans from the Farm Credit Corporation. In Ontario farm operations in arrears
increased by 161, while in the province of Quebec the increase was 108.
These are very disturbing statistics, especially when one considers that there has already been a dramatic decrease in the number of farmers in Canada over the past four decades. In 1941, for example, there were 3.2 million farmers comprising 27.4 per cent of the total Canadian population. In 1976, there were only one million farmers, comprising 4.6 per cent of Canada's population. Of course, with this trend continuing, these figures would be much lower today.
I fear that the government's high interest rate policies will hasten this decline because the young farmers, the future of Canadian agriculture, are the ones who are suffering the most from these policies. If Canada loses its young farmers, it also loses its security of a stable and constant food supply in the future. This affects each and every one of us as Canadians, as well as people beyond our borders.
Canadian agriculture needs the help of the federal government in meeting this interest rate crisis. 1 have developed a ten-point plan of action to help the farm sector, and we on this side urge the government to give this plan very serious consideration.
First, the government should grant the Farm Credit Corporation immediately an additional $150 million. The Ontario Federation of Agriculture and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have recommended that this be done. It should be noted that we faced the same problem when we were in government in 1979. Nevertheless, we were able to find an additional $50 million to keep the corporation going.
Second, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should reconsider his attitude toward farm credit interest rates. One of his first actions upon being restored as Minister of Agriculture in March, 1980, was to increase the interest rate to 13 per cent. He set an all-time record. He was not satisfied with that, and on April 1, 1980, he again raised the rates to an all-time high in the 51 or 52-year history of the Farm Credit Corporation to 14 per cent. By choosing April Fool's Day for his announcement, the minister is only fooling himself if he believes that this record high interest rate will benefit Canadian agriculture.
I mentioned earlier that farm bankruptcies, foreclosures, forced sales and debt arrears have been increasing daily across Canada. The new farm credit interest rate will not help that situation. It will also discourage many young people from going into farming as a career, and it will discourage many established farmers from expanding their existing operations.
Third, the minister should introduce the necessary legislation which would allow the corporation to borrow supplementary funds from the private marketplace. This legislation has been promised for the past three years. Had it been in place three years ago, many farmers might not be suffering to the same degree that they are now.
Fourth, the provisions of the small business development bond ought to be extended to unincorporated farmers. The bond, first made public in the Crosbie budget, offered low
May 13, 1981

interest rates to small businessmen and to incorporated farmers who wished to expand their operations. Extending its provisions would help to reduce the level of demand on the Farm Credit Corporation, because 60 per cent of farm credit loans go toward farm expansion. Since most tax relief measures apply equally to incorporated and unincorporated farmers, the provisions of the small business development bond should be extended to unincorporated farmers.
Fifth, the federal stabilization program should be improved. At present, the stabilization payments come too late to be of maximum benefit to affect farmers. In many cases farmers, who are eligible for stabilization payments, have to borrow short-term money now at rates of 21 per cent or 22 per cent in order to pay for replacement of livestock, feed, seed, fertilizer and other day to day input costs.
The 1979-1980 hog stabilization program is an excellent example of the need for improvement. Some stabilization payments did not reach the hog producers until six months after the date on which they had applied. This has been especially unfortunate because hog producers have been one of the commodity groups hardest hit by the combination of high interest rates and low prices. Beef producers have suffered severely by finding themselves caught in the same bind.
Sixth, the minister should adopt the recommendation of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture which calls for the establishment of an independent review agency to look at each case before the banks could foreclose on a farm operation. This proposal should be extended to include all lending institutions, perhaps even to include the Farm Credit Corporation, although I must say their policy does contain far more compassion, reason and understanding than do those of most traditional lending agencies in this country.
Seventh, the Minister of Agriculture should, together with his provincial colleagues and representatives of the agricultural industry across Canada, develop-not simply get together and have a meeting and discuss the situation which occurred in Ottawa yesterday-a common approach for assisting the farm community in surviving the high interest rate problem. Because of the lack of action on the part of the federal government in solving or alleviating the interest rate crisis, they have no choice but to turn to their provincial governments.
In Ontario, for example, the OFA has called upon the provincial government to set up an interest rate assistance plan covering loans from both banks and farm suppliers to a maximum of $150,000. The plan would be based on a graduated scale. Farmers who owned less than half of their farm would receive 100 per cent of everything that the bank charged over a 12 per cent interest rate. Farmers with 90 per cent to 100 per cent equity would be subsidized at the rate of 20 per cent on everything charged over 12 per cent. Payments would be made quarterly.
My concern about such proposals is that there could be ten different assistance programs across Canada and the result could be highly discriminatory. Therefore, we urge the minis-
Interest Rates
ter to take a leadership role, together with his provincial colleagues, and develop a national plan of action.
Our eighth point is one of encouraging the Canadian lending institutions to be more responsive to the borrowing needs of farmers. I have noted that the Minister of Agriculture has raised this point with the Canadian chartered banks, and I want to congratulate him for his initiative. I hope he will continue to work in concert, not only with the banks but with all institutions involved in farm financing in order that a loan system can be structured to meet the long-term needs of Canadian agriculture.
The federal cabinet has to be made aware that action with respect to this problem is needed and it is needed now. I am distressed by the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture that the solution to high interest rates lies solely with the banks. In an April 18 interview on CBC Radio, the minister said:
That's why I'm suggesting that I think the banking institutions have a public responsibility to make sure that that production entity for the total good of society stays alive.
I believe the minister is putting the cart before the horse. I always thought it was the banks which responded to government policy direction, not the other way around. Therefore I do not think the Minister of Agriculture can wash his hands of the problem by saying that it is a banking problem, not a government policy problem.
The Minister of Agriculture should be able to have some influence in shaping government policy in relation to interest rates because he is a long-time member of cabinet. He should be able to persuade his cabinet colleagues to bring forward the positive measures which farm groups have proposed and we have proposed in today's debate. However, we recognize the minister's problem: he has no clout in cabinet.
The minister should not hide his head in the sand and complain that the interest rate problem is a banking problem and that its solution lies with the banks absorbing any losses on farm loans. The banks have a role in solving the problem, but high interest rates are a deliberate federal government policy decision. As such, the federal government must take a major responsibility in alleviating the financial hardships which unfairly strike certain sectors of the economy.
As the voice in cabinet for Canadian agriculture, the Minister of Agriculture must recognize that young farmers and some commodity groups like hogs and beef producers are suffering extreme financial hardships because of high interest rates. They deserve help, and they need help now.
In closing, and it brings me to my final point, I again remind this government, and particularly the Minister of Agriculture, that his failure to deal with this problem is not a recent one. Rather, the minister will recall making a commitment to do something at least to help Canadian farmers. He made that commitment here in Ottawa to 1,000 farmers. I was there. That commitment was not made yesterday, a week ago or a month ago, but rather in Ottawa in January, 1980, 16 months ago.

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
The fact is that interest rates since that time have increased by 50 per cent and the minister has produced absolutely nothing. The agricultural industry is of vital importance to our Canadian economy. One in every four, 25 per cent of Canadians are employed either directly or indirectly in the agricultural and food industry. Agriculture is everyone's bread and butter.
If the Minister of Agriculture continues to simply talk, talk which borders on political mischief, and delivers nothing, if the minister refuses to recognize that high interest rates are a deliberate government policy, if he continues to refuse to accept his responsibility for resolving this problem, then he should do the honourable thing and resign. What the Canadian agricultural industry requires now, more than any time in our history, is not simply a loud voice, but rather some real action.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNPRECEDENTED HIGH LEVELS OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again it is a great pleasure and an honour for me to take the floor today in the House to debate a subject which affects us all to various degrees; I refer to the interest rates or the prime rate of the Bank of Canada as defined in this country.
The House is now studying a motion introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) who, in a few words, condemns the minister because, it would seem, he shows apathy, fails to hold discussions and shirks his responsibilities. In my opinion it is altogether dishonest to convey such an image to the people. Being a former finance minister the hon. member for St. John's West ought to know that the role of a finance minister is not limited to reviewing the over-all economic situation of a country. He has to know what is happening in every home in every country of the world as a starting point to establishing a general strategy based on several months or several years of observation with a view to solving the major economic problems.
Of course, as the member for the riding of Lac-Saint-Jean, I hail from a region where interest rates are particularly high, since it is one of the most severely affected areas in the province of Quebec. When a small businessman has to pay high interest rates on his bank credit margin and when a company is forced to borrow at such rates, it does affect job creation to a certain extent. But worse still it is again the sales market which by far has to come to grips with the direct consequences of all those problems. In addition, a segment of the population must, of course, pay the costs of high interest rates. The home owner who is facing a mortgage renewal has to expect to pay higher rates than he is doing now. Given current conditions it seems to me there is no way out, that is part of the drawback of having to borrow to make a purchase. Someone who borrows but has the money to buy does not suffer this hardship, but the one who has to borrow to purchase something is at the mercy of the person who makes the money available to him as required.
What I am getting at, Mr. Speaker, is that there are some things which the members opposite seem to have forgotten. Those things are, in my view, of utmost importance, as they are the very basis of our society. It is true that we are faced today with sky-high interest rates. I agree. But there is a much greater problem that has been facing us for years and is still facing us, that is unemployment. There are numerous jobless in this country, especially among the young.
That is the point I wanted to make. Coming from a region where unemployment is almost at 20 per cent, I know that 60 per cent of our unemployed are young people just out of school, just out of university, or who did not have the opportunity to pursue their studies very far, and they have to cope with this problem.
On the positive side of the Minister of Finance's record for the last year and a half, it must be recognized that for the first time in five years the unemployment rate has dropped significantly, that is 0.7 per cent in one year. Those are tangible results. I think that the unemployment problem is a much more serious one than the temporary one of high interest rates. Let me briefly explain why: the young person who is unemployed or on welfare is unable to borrow, whether the interest rate is 10 per cent or 18 per cent. It is simply impossible for him or her to borrow money because, as we all know, to borrow money you must have money or at least some assets. I am not at all surprised to hear my colleagues opposite say that those who have assets or money cannot borrow at such rates. I agree. But for some workers, it is even more difficult. Someone who has been living in a house for ten years and must now renew his mortgage will have to pay a bit more for a little while, probably for one year, and at worst let us say for two years. However, the fact is that most Canadian workers are able to face this problem and tighten their belts a bit.
And I am asking them to do so, not in a masochistic context but because it is the only solution now available to fight inflation which affects the poor, those who must buy coffee or oil or oranges or any one of a vast number of other imported products every day. The worst thing that we could do to them would be to devaluate the dollar. The former minister of finance is well aware that when the interest rates are lower in Canada than in the United States, the value of the Canadian dollar drops, and this means that the people without much money, such as the unemployed, and those on welfare, will have to spend even more for food, for heat, for clothing, for all the basic necessities of life.
It is true that our government has made a choice. And it says here that the Minister of Finance has permitted interest rates to rise. It is true! By doing so, what has the government done? It has taken its responsibilities. Why did it do so? First of all, to stop inflation which affects the most needy, the poorest in our society.
May 13, 1981

Second, it is true that we are harming to a certain extent one sector of the population, the average income earners, since they will have to tighten their belts for a limited time.
It still remains that as members of Parliament in this country, as a group of citizens, we have to take our responsibilities toward the young people who have been coming out of our schools for a number of years and facing what? Very strong unions who have provided job security for certain employees who are now 55 years old on average. There are very few jobs for young people because they lack experience. Because we wanted to protect the worker, we have created a blind alley which deprives our young people of the same opportunities as their predecessors. We have to realize that these young people are living in a world where ownership is important. In Canada, nearly everyone owns a piece of land, a house, or at least a car, and maybe also a cottage, a snowmobile, a fur coat-I could go on with this list for hours. Very few countries in the world have given this opportunity to their citizens.
We are now saying to one sector of our society: You will have to tighten your belt somewhat because we have to provide for our young people, for the next generation. If we are to prevent those people from being frustrated, it must be recognized now that somewhat higher interest rates will have to be paid so that in their turn things will be somewhat less expensive, because often all they can afford is oranges and coffee. This is about all they get from our society, with some occasional help from their parents in order to make ends meet or to buy some durable good that others can afford regularly. That must be understood.
What must be overcome over the next few years is that kind of unemployment, unless we want to find ourselves in a few years with a class of frustrated people, with two different generations, one living in very small rental apartments, looking at the other class in large homes. If that is what we are looking for in this country, let us keep in mind right now that tomorrow's young people will point their fingers at us and say: The billions you thought you were putting aside for your pension plans, we feel we are entitled to use them now. Because I have a social conscience, I must state that for some time I, as a consumer, will buy somewhat less because of high interest rates. I do not believe people live in misery, because there was a time not so long ago, where interest rates were at reasonable levels, let us say 9 per cent or 10 per cent. Did that help our unemployed buy homes? Did that help people without income to live in luxury? Did it make it easier for them to borrow from the banks? No! They never had any chance with the banks. Because what they need is guaranteed survival, work, an income they can depend on year after year. And this will certainly not be achieved by blaming it on American interest rates.
If Western Germany, considered one of the strongest countries in the Western World, cannot stop inflation nor withstand
Interest Rates
the pressure of American rates on the German mark, how could we here succeed when so much of our goods come from the United States? Do we want to see billions of Canadian dollars fleeing south to the United States overnight? Is that our goal, the fall of our dollar? If that is the goal, let us follow the suggestion made by the former minister of finance. We could then say we had no choice, we had to assist home owners with their payments. Admittedly they are a burden. But, as a society, should we not at some point take the time to turn and look back at those who follow us? Should we not at some point tell our children: We will try to give you the same opportunities your fathers had. Our fathers could not borrow easily just anywhere. They did not build themselves empires, grand mansions. Nor did they have huge cars. They did not own all the material goods we have. Who benefited from their efforts? Who benefited from the wages they earned? Who benefited from the sacrifices they made unless we did? Who had jobs when they left school if not ourselves? And that is the important point, Mr. Speaker. The future of a country is not built on the present but on what lies ahead, the future. The present is only what we are living. It is the time for action, granted. But those who will build the Canada of tomorrow are those we are preparing mentally. Granted, I am willing to say that in years past the government made efforts to at least help the young to keep their self-respect. We gave them-and some blamed us for doing so-we gave them, as I was saying, $130 a week in unemployment insurance to enable them to at least treat themselves to a beer and a laugh once in a while, and to buy food. That was important, because when one cannot pay for one's food, one loses all self-respect, one feels hurt. It is true also that we have created temporary jobs. I remember quite well when the Clark government decided to get rid of the Canada Works program and other job-creation projects. For what purpose? Supposedly to set up stronger economic structures. But why was it established if not for those young people who with the $100 paid to them every week-which is much less than the average wage paid in Canada-could at least manage to salvage part of their self-respect? It had to be done and it was done, but this scheme could not be expected to last for years. As the government, we are beginning to talk about economic restructuring. We are starting to look ahead to the future with computerized industries, advanced technology, the development of our own energy resources and the full utilization of our millions of square kilometres of territory for the benefit of 26 million Canadians. But in order to reach this goal we need a few months or perhaps a year of small sacrifices on the part of a population which for 20 years at least, more so than any other people in the world, has enjoyed consumer goods and facilities to raise their children and live in this country.
The present generation must be ready today to pay at least a fraction of what our fathers paid to help young people get out of the hole which has been dug for them by union rights given to workers, which was legitimate, by industries that failed to

May 13, 1981
Interest Rates
modernize their facilities fast enough because large dividends were paid to shareholders who could be anybody. Finally, for all sorts of reasons, that is quite normal, Mr. Speaker.
This is why I cannot agree with the hon. member for St. John's West when he says that the minister has not met his responsibilities as Minister of Finance. It is quite the contrary. Just as past ministers of finance, the present Minister of Finance, under the leadership of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), has worked along similar lines to build the future of this country. When the time came to support our young people the Liberal finance ministers introduced legislation to do so. Today we say: Let us follow the American policy of high interest rates, let us pay the price for a while, but let us reduce the unemployment rate, make more jobs available to our young people, give them more job opportunities and especially let us control inflation which always hits the underprivileged harder so that the country will not become a living hell for the poor while the rich people continue to spend. In short, this is what I had to say, Mr. Speaker, and indeed I ask
my constituents in Lac-Saint-Jean to do what I am prepared to do myself, that is, to accept for a limited time higher interest rates. I ask them to do so for the sake of those who built our country and who are now retired and often have but the bare minimum to live on, for the sake of those who have left us when their job was done and finally for the sake of our children who will carry on. It would be totally stupid today to continue to concentrate everything on our generation when so much wealth, lands and so many assets are available to all our people. The essential thing is to share with those who will succeed us as our fathers have shared with us.
